title: Toolkit — vol to moves, vol cones, hedged P&L, Kelly sizing, vol drag
lede: Five calculators to keep open beside a screen. Each one is a page of the series turned into something you can type your own numbers into, with the page it comes from linked so the reasoning is one click away.

chapters.title: Turn a vol into a move before anyone finishes the sentence
chapters.dek: Annual vol over sixteen is a daily move. Everything else is the same square root.

figures.title: One-sigma move against horizon
figures.caption: Notice how far the blue curve sits above the grey line at the short end. Uncertainty arrives front-loaded: a quarter of the year carries half of the year's standard deviation.

figures.title: Cheat sheet — one-sigma move as a percent of spot

chapters.text: A volatility quote is a standard deviation per year. To use it you need it per day, per week, per expiry, and in dollars. The square root of time does all of it, and √252 ≈ 16 is close enough that a 32-vol stock moves about 2% a day and a 16-vol index about 1%. Page 01 derives the √T; page 18 explains why the straddle's move is only 80% of a standard deviation. One-sigma move against horizon Your stock, by horizon The quote Notice how far the blue curve sits above the grey line at the short end. Uncertainty arrives front-loaded: a quarter of the year carries half of the year's standard deviation. [equation: daily move ≈ σ / 16 · move over T ≈ S · σ · √T] Reads as: divide the annual vol by sixteen for a day, and scale by the square root of the time for anything else. Cheat sheet — one-sigma move as a percent of spot Print it and tape it to the monitor.

chapters.title: Is this vol high? Only against its own history
chapters.dek: A vol cone puts today's realized vol at every lookback inside the range it has lived in. Implied gets judged against that, not against a feeling.

figures.title: Realized-vol cone
figures.caption: The demo series has a calm stretch, a stressed one and a recovery, which is why its cone is wide at the short end. Notice where the blue line sits: realized vol at short lookbacks is noisy enough that a single reading proves little, which is why the median and quartiles are the reference, not the latest print.

terms.Vol cone: The minimum, quartiles, median and maximum of rolling realized volatility at several lookback windows. Short windows swing widely and long ones narrowly, so the bands form a cone.

chapters.text: "Thirty vol is expensive" means nothing until you know what thirty vol is for this name. A vol cone answers it. Take a history of closes, compute rolling realized vol over 10, 21, 42, 63, 126 and 252 days, and for each window record the range it has spanned. Short windows swing wildly and long ones barely move, so the bands narrow into a cone. Then lay two things over it: where each window's realized vol sits today, and the implied vol you are being quoted. Implied near the top of the cone at the matching tenor is rich against history; near the bottom, cheap. Sinclair's work on volatility trading popularized the tool, and it is still the fastest honest answer to "is this high". Paste any column of closes below — a CSV with dates works, because the last number on each line is read as the close. Realized-vol cone Compare The demo series has a calm stretch, a stressed one and a recovery, which is why its cone is wide at the short end. Notice where the blue line sits: realized vol at short lookbacks is noisy enough that a single reading proves little, which is why the median and quartiles are the reference, not the latest print. [equation: σ_realized(w) = √( 252 · Var[ ln(Sₜ / Sₜ₋₁) ] over the last w days )] Reads as: the standard deviation of daily log returns over the window, annualized by √252. Page 18 covers what changes if you use absolute returns instead.

chapters.title: What a hedged option earns if your vol view is right
chapters.dek: Buy at implied, hedge daily, and the expected P&L is the gap between realized and implied variance , scaled by vega.

figures.title: Expected P&L of a long, delta-hedged ATM option, against realized vol
figures.caption: Notice the blue curve bends above the grey line on both sides. The long option gains more for each extra point of realized vol than it loses for each point short — the variance convexity of page 11 showing up in an ordinary option.

chapters.text: A delta-hedged long option earns ½Γ(ΔS)² on each move and pays theta for it. Theta is set by the implied vol you paid; the gamma income is set by the vol that actually happens. Average it out and the expected P&L is vega × (σ_r² − σ_i²)/(2σ_i) — close to vega times the vol difference for small gaps, and convex for large ones because the payoff is in variance. Two caveats to carry. This is an expectation : page 25 chapter 07 shows the same realized vol paying anywhere from −2.61 to +6.12 depending on when it arrives relative to your gamma. And it assumes the option stays near the money; far from the strike, gamma fades and so does the income. Expected P&L of a long, delta-hedged ATM option, against realized vol The trade Notice the blue curve bends above the grey line on both sides. The long option gains more for each extra point of realized vol than it loses for each point short — the variance convexity of page 11 showing up in an ordinary option. [equation: E[P&L] ≈ vega · (σ_r² − σ_i²) / (2σ_i)] Reads as: you are paid the difference in variances, converted into vol points through vega. Short the option and the sign flips.

chapters.title: Having an edge is half of it; sizing is the other half
chapters.dek: An option bet with a positive expectation can still ruin you if it is too large. The Kelly fraction is the size that maximizes long-run growth.

figures.title: Long-run growth rate against the fraction bet
figures.caption: Notice the curve is flat at the top and steep on the right. Undersizing costs little; oversizing costs a lot, and far enough past Kelly a winning bet loses money over time.

terms.Kelly criterion: The bet size that maximizes the expected logarithm of wealth, and so the long-run growth rate. Betting more than Kelly lowers growth while raising risk; most practitioners bet a fraction of it.

chapters.text: Price a structure as a bet: it costs c and pays W if you are right. The market's implied probability is c/W. If you believe a higher probability p, you have an edge — and the question every trader underweights is how much of the bankroll to put on it. The Kelly criterion answers: bet f* = p − (1 − p)/b, where b = (W − c)/c is the payout odds. Growth rises to a peak at f* and falls away on both sides. For a small, even-odds edge, twice Kelly gives back all of the growth and half Kelly keeps three-quarters of it; for a long-shot payoff the curve is lopsided — on this trade half Kelly keeps 86% — but the penalty for oversizing always arrives. Because your p is an estimate, most practitioners bet a fraction of Kelly. The default here is page 15 's biotech trade: a 10/5 put spread at $0.19 that pays $5 if the failure price is as bad as your team thinks. Long-run growth rate against the fraction bet The bet Notice the curve is flat at the top and steep on the right. Undersizing costs little; oversizing costs a lot, and far enough past Kelly a winning bet loses money over time. [equation: f* = p − (1 − p) / b · g(f) = p·ln(1 + f·b) + (1 − p)·ln(1 − f)] Reads as: bet your edge divided by the odds; growth is the probability-weighted log of what happens to your bankroll. The statistics underneath Expectation and bet sizing ↗ , in Chance, visually, derives the Kelly fraction this calculator uses.

chapters.title: Volatility is a cost to anyone who compounds
chapters.dek: The median investor earns the average return minus half the variance. Lever it daily and the drag grows with the square of the leverage.

figures.title: Median wealth over time
figures.caption: Notice the blue line separates from the gold one even when the index goes nowhere in particular. Raise the vol and the leveraged fund's median can fall while the index's rises: the fund is short the variance it rebalances against.

chapters.text: Up 50% then down 50% leaves you at 75%. Volatility pulls compounded growth below the arithmetic average by about σ²/2 a year — the same −σ²/2 that sits in page 01 's lognormal. It is why the median outcome lags the mean, and why reducing volatility at the same average return raises wealth. A leveraged ETF resets to its multiple every day, so its compounded growth is Lμ − L²σ²/2. Compare that with L times the index's growth and the difference is −(L² − L)σ²/2: a drag that grows with the square of the leverage and the square of the vol. At 20 vol, a 3× fund loses about 12% a year to it — more than many years' worth of the index's excess return. Inverse funds pay it too, and more: a −1× fund has L² − L = 2. Median wealth over time The fund Notice the blue line separates from the gold one even when the index goes nowhere in particular. Raise the vol and the leveraged fund's median can fall while the index's rises: the fund is short the variance it rebalances against. [equation: growth ≈ μ − σ²/2 · L× daily reset: Lμ − L²σ²/2] Reads as: volatility costs half its square in growth, and leverage multiplies the return by L but the cost by L². Continuous rebalancing and lognormal returns are assumed; fees and financing make it worse.
